parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A student phones a garden centre to ask about a part-time weekend job.
script: Good morning, Fernhill Garden Centre, Greg speaking.
Oh, hello. I saw an advert on the noticeboard in the library about a weekend job at your garden centre, and I'm calling to find out if it's still available.
It is, yes. Now, are you thinking of the job on the tills? We had two of those, but I'm afraid they've both gone.
Oh, I see. Well, I'm happy to do anything, really. What's left?

We're still looking for a nursery assistant. That means looking after the plants in the greenhouses and out on the sales benches, so watering, labelling, tidying, and helping customers to carry things to their cars. Have you done anything like that before?
A bit. I've been helping my grandfather on his allotment since I was about ten, and last summer I worked at a farm shop, mostly stacking vegetables and serving.
That sounds ideal, actually. Let me take a few details so I can put you on the list for an interview. Can I have your name?
It's Jessica Hargreaves. People often put two Es in the middle, but it's H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E-S.
Hargreaves, got it. And is there a phone number where we can reach you?
07712 408 336. Lovely. Now, the job is Saturdays and Sundays. We used to ask for Friday evenings as well, but we don't need that any more, so it's just the weekend. Is that all right for you?
Weekends are perfect. I have lectures during the week. What time would I be working?
Well, we open to customers at 9 and close at 5, but the nursery staff work from 8.30 until 4.30, because the people on the tills do the closing up.
That's fine. And what's the pay like?
It's 11 pounds 40 an hour for the first three months. After that it goes up to 12 pounds, but you'd start on the lower rate, I'm afraid.
That's fine, thank you. Is there a uniform?
Yes, we give you a green fleece and a polo shirt, so you don't need to buy anything except a decent pair of boots. The greenhouse floors can get quite wet.
I've got some of those already. Good.
Right, the next step is an interview. The nursery manager likes to meet everybody in person. Could you come on Wednesday?
Oh, I have a seminar on Wednesday afternoon, sorry. Would Thursday be possible?
Let me have a look. Thursday should be fine, yes, she's in all day on Thursday. How about 2 o'clock?
I have a class that finishes at 2, and it's a ten-minute bus ride to you, so could we say a quarter past?

2.15, then. No problem. Now, please bring something to show that you're allowed to work in this country. Your passport is the easiest thing. A reference would be helpful too, but you don't have to have one on the day.
I've got my passport, and I'll bring a reference from the farm shop as well, if that's all right.
Is there anywhere to park? Or should I come on the bus?
There's a big car park at the front, and it's free for staff and for people coming for interviews. The number 14 bus stops right outside the gate, though, if you'd rather do that.
I'll probably take the bus. Who should I ask for when I arrive?
Ask at the main desk for Mrs Pemberton. That's P-E-M-B-E-R-T-O-N. She's the nursery manager, and she'll show you round the greenhouses before the interview, so you can see what you'd be doing.
Brilliant. Thank you very much, Greg. I'm really looking forward to it.
Our pleasure, Jessica. See you on Thursday. Bye for now.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: The project manager of a new community arts centre gives a talk to local residents at the opening evening.
script: Good evening, everyone, and thank you so much for coming along. My name's Ngaio Reid, and I'm the project manager for the Tidewater Arts Centre. I'm going to tell you a little about how the centre came about and how you can get involved, and then I'll take you on a quick tour before we have refreshments in the café.

First, the building. A lot of people assume it was a cinema, because of the tall windows and the big hall at the front, and some of the older residents tell me they remember a warehouse on this site. In fact it was Tidewater Primary School, which closed in 2009. For years it stood empty, and by 2017 the council was considering pulling it down. A group of residents, led by a retired teacher called Alan Morgan, persuaded the council to wait while they came up with a plan.

Paying for that plan was the hard part. The total cost came to just over 2 million pounds. The council contributed about a quarter of that, and I'm proud to say that local people raised nearly a fifth through donations, bake sales and a sponsored swim. But the biggest share, just over half, was a grant from the National Lottery fund, and without it the project simply would not have happened.

Some of you will remember that we were due to open last January. Well, the roof turned out to be in much better condition than we had feared, and the builders found nothing wrong with the foundations either. What held us up was the wiring. When the electricians opened up the walls, they found cables dating from the 1960s that were quite unsafe, and the whole building had to be rewired. That took four months, which is why we are opening now, in May, and not in January.

Now, how can you use the centre? Everything here is open to the public. You can walk into the gallery or the café without paying anything, and tickets for concerts and films are available to anybody. But if you'd like to join our classes, you'll need to become a member. Membership is 25 pounds a year, and it takes 15 per cent off all class fees. We also have patron members, who pay 80 pounds a year and get priority booking for popular courses, but for most people the standard membership is all about the discount.

We run on a very small budget, so volunteers matter enormously. The café is run by a small paid team, and I'm pleased to say that we already have more volunteer guides for the gallery than we have visitors to guide. What we really need is people to help with the children's workshops on Saturday mornings. You don't need any experience, just patience and a sense of humour. There's a sign-up sheet by the door.

Right, let me tell you what's where, and then we'll walk round together. As you come in from Quay Road, you're standing in the Harbour Room, which used to be the school's entrance hall. It has high ceilings and long white walls, so we'll use it for exhibitions, and our first show, by local photographers, is already hung. The film screenings will not be in here, by the way. They'll be in the main hall at the back, which has the raised stage, and you'll see that at the end of the tour.

On your left is the Lantern Room, named after the lantern-shaped skylight in its ceiling. It's the brightest room in the building and it has wipe-clean floors, so it's going to be used for children's painting classes. We had originally planned to run sewing and textiles there, but the demand for painting was so strong that the textile group has moved to a room upstairs for now.

Past the stairs, you'll find the Copper Room. The kilns are in there, which is why the walls are fireproof, and you can see the potters' wheels along the window. That's where our ceramics classes will take place, on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

If you go upstairs, the large room under the roof is called the Loft. It has a sprung wooden floor and mirrors along one wall, and it will be used for dance classes, everything from ballet for beginners to salsa on Friday nights.

And finally, at the back of the courtyard is the Boiler House. It was the school's boiler room, with thick brick walls, and we realised that was perfect for sound. So it's been turned into a rehearsal space for musicians, and bands will be able to book it by the hour. Neighbours will not hear a thing, I promise.

So that's the building. If you'd like to follow me, we'll start in the Harbour Room, and I'll answer any questions as we go. And please do help yourselves to refreshments when we get to the café at the end. Thank you.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students discuss an exhibition they visited for a museum studies assignment.
script: Okay, Callum, so we've got until Friday to hand in the evaluation of the exhibition. Shall we go through our notes from the visit and decide what to write?
Yes, good idea. I've got my phone full of photos, and I made some rough notes on the train home. Where do you want to start?
Maybe with why we picked it. I know you said it was free for students.
It was, and it's only ten minutes from campus, which is handy.

True, but I'd put it differently in the report. I suggested the Voices of the River exhibition because it won that national design award last month, and a prize-winning exhibition makes a good test of what good display actually looks like.
Right, fair enough. Free entry was just a bonus, then.
Exactly. Now, the entrance. I thought the ticket desk was fine, actually. Nobody queued for long.

Yes, the queue wasn't the problem. It was after the desk that things went wrong. I stood in the foyer for about a minute, and I had no idea which way to go. There were doors left and right, and nothing telling you where the exhibition began.
That's true. I only found the start because I followed a family. We should definitely say the signs were unclear.
Agreed. And what did you make of the audio guide?

Mixed, really. The content is great. The old fishermen speaking about the floods, that kind of thing. But each recording runs for about three minutes, and standing in front of a case for that long, you feel a bit stuck. I saw people take their headphones off after the first one.
I thought the sound quality was good, and the children's version looked fun.
Yes, those are fine. It's the length I'd criticise.
Okay. What about the touchscreens? I wasn't impressed.
No, and a couple of them were switched off, I think.

Were they? I thought they were just slow to wake up. Once you touched them they worked, but they took ages to respond to every touch. I tried to flick through the old photographs and the screen lagged each time.
Oh, I see. So not so much broken as sluggish. Good point. I'll write that they were slow to respond.
Right. Let's do the grid, then. Layout first. I thought at first it was a straight line, but when I looked at the plan afterwards, it's actually a loop.

Yes, circular, so you end up back at the foyer, which works well because nobody gets lost once they've started. Next, the text panels. They were full of technical terms, which a general visitor can't follow.
No, technical is the right word. Terms like hydrology and sediment, with no explanation. Then the lighting. I thought at first the problem was shadows, because some objects were hard to see.
But it's the glass cases, isn't it? You see the reflections of the spotlights and your own face instead of the objects.
That's what it was. Reflections, definitely. I'll fix that in my notes.
What would you say was the strongest display?
The model of the old ferry. The bridge model was bigger, but you couldn't get close to it, whereas the ferry had a little cabin you could look inside.
I'd go for the ferry as well. What was missing, though, was something for visitors with hearing difficulties. The films have captions, but there's nothing written to go with the audio guide.
No, there aren't any transcripts. That's an obvious gap, and it wouldn't be hard to put right.
And my last point is that you walk for nearly two hours, and I counted only three benches in the whole place.
Yes, I'll put that in the recommendations. More seating, definitely. I'd say that's the cheapest improvement they could make.
Good. Shall I draft the first section tonight and send it to you in the morning?
Perfect. I'll write the part about the audio guide and the touchscreens, and then we can swap and edit each other's work.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about volcanoes and soil fertility.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to look at a paradox. A volcano can destroy a village in an afternoon, and yet for thousands of years people have chosen to farm on volcanic slopes. Hundreds of millions of people live within a hundred kilometres of an active volcano, and many of them are there for one simple reason: the soil. So what makes volcanic soil so good, and why does it come with such risks?

Let's start with what an eruption actually puts on the land. Most of it is ash, which is tiny fragments of volcanic glass and crystals. When ash is fresh, it's chemically rich. It's a particularly good source of phosphorus, which is the nutrient that helps roots to develop, and many ordinary soils are short of it. But fresh ash can't be used by plants straight away. The nutrients are locked inside the glass, and they're released only as the ash weathers.

The speed of weathering depends on the climate. In dry regions it can take centuries before an ash layer turns into good soil. But in warm, wet, tropical regions it can happen far faster, within a few decades. That's one reason why some of the most densely populated places on earth are on the slopes of tropical volcanoes. The classic example is the island of Java, in Indonesia. Farmers there have grown rice on volcanic soils for over a thousand years, on terraces cut into the mountainsides, and some fields give two or even three harvests a year.

Chemistry isn't the whole story, though. The structure of the soil matters as much. As ash weathers, it forms a mineral with a very open, sponge-like structure. It's called allophane, and I'll spell that for you: A-L-L-O-P-H-A-N-E. Allophane holds on to water extremely well, and it also holds nutrients so that rain doesn't wash them away. The result is a soil that is light, easy to dig, and able to supply plants through a dry spell.

Now for the other side of the paradox. Fresh ash can bury a crop. A light dusting, two or three centimetres, is usually harmless and can even be a benefit, because it acts like a mulch and adds minerals. But once the layer is deeper than about 15 centimetres, seedlings are smothered and even established plants can be broken by the weight, particularly if the ash gets wet. It takes a field years to recover from that kind of burial.

There's a second problem. Fresh ash contains almost no nitrogen, since nitrogen comes mainly from living things, and nothing has lived there yet. Farmers deal with this in different ways. Some bring in manure or compost, but the cheapest and most common solution is to plant legumes, such as beans or peas, which take nitrogen from the air and enrich the soil themselves.

Not all the benefits of volcanoes come from ash. In Iceland, where the growing season is short and the climate is cold, farmers use greenhouses heated by geothermal energy, that is, heat from underground. Tomatoes and cucumbers are grown there all year round, which would be unthinkable otherwise.

Let me turn now to some recent research. Dr Maren Holt and her team studied farms in the Andes at different distances from an active crater. You might expect the farms closest to the volcano to do best, since they get the most ash. In fact, they didn't. Yields were low close to the crater, where ash was deep and the air contained acid gases that damaged the crops. They were also low in farms more than fifty kilometres away, where the ash layer was too thin to make a difference. The highest yields were in the middle, between about twenty and thirty kilometres from the crater.

That leaves the question of danger. We can now monitor many volcanoes closely, and warning systems exist. You might think that the main obstacle would be cost, or lack of technology. In reality, the difficulty is trust. After a false alarm, when families have left their homes and nothing has happened, many farmers are reluctant to evacuate the next time. Livestock, equipment and a harvest are at stake, and people have to be convinced that the risk is real.

So what should we conclude? I'd suggest that we shouldn't treat the fertility of volcanic land and the danger of living on it as two separate issues. Banning farming near volcanoes is neither realistic nor fair, and fertilisers cannot replace what these soils provide to millions of people. The sensible approach is for planners to consider the benefits and the risks together, deciding where to farm, how to warn people, and how to help communities recover. Thank you. I'll take questions now.

passages.title: The Cold Chain
paras: A  For most of history, keeping food from spoiling meant stopping it from being the food it was. Salting, smoking, drying and pickling all preserved meat, fish and vegetables, but they changed the flavour and texture of whatever was kept, and none of them could keep a fresh peach or a jug of milk for more than a few days. Cold was the exception. A cellar dug deep into the ground, or a pit packed with winter snow, would slow decay without altering taste. Wealthy European households built ice houses in their gardens, while farmers in colder regions cut blocks from frozen lakes and stored them under straw. Yet natural cold was available only to people who lived near it and who owned the land or the labour to harvest it, and for the great majority of families a cold drink in summer remained out of reach.

B  The first person to see ice as a commodity rather than a luxury was a New England merchant, Amos Garrick, who in the 1820s began cutting ice from the ponds near his home and selling it in warmer places. Sceptics laughed: ice, they said, would melt long before it arrived. They were partly right. Garrick's early cargoes lost more than half of their weight on the voyage, and he learned to pack the blocks in sawdust, which insulated them far better than straw, and to ship them in thick-walled holds. Within thirty years the trade employed tens of thousands of cutters, sailors and dock workers, and ice was being delivered to ports as distant as Calcutta. For the first time, a restaurant in a hot city could keep fish fresh and serve cold drinks throughout the summer.

C  The ice trade's greatest rivals were not other merchants but engineers. In the 1850s, several inventors built machines that cooled by compressing a gas and then letting it expand, drawing heat from the surroundings in the process. The first buyers were not households but breweries. Lager, a beer that must ferment at low temperatures, had been brewed only in winter or in cellars chilled with natural ice, and a machine allowed brewers to make it all year round. Meatpackers followed, and so did ice factories, which could produce clear blocks from clean water in any climate. Even so, natural ice remained cheaper in many places, and cutters continued to harvest ponds well into the early twentieth century.

D  Machines made it possible to move meat across oceans. In the early 1880s, a sailing ship fitted with a cooling chamber carried frozen mutton from the far southern hemisphere to London. The meat arrived in good condition, and a trade that had seemed fantastic suddenly looked profitable. Within a decade, refrigerated steamers were bringing beef, lamb, butter and apples to European ports, and sheep and cattle farmers on the other side of the world had access to a market of millions. In Britain, imported meat was cheaper than home-produced meat, and families in industrial towns, who had rarely eaten it, began to do so regularly. Not everyone welcomed the change: British farmers complained that cheap imports threatened their livelihood and campaigned for restrictions, with little success.

E  The domestic refrigerator arrived later and more slowly. Early electric models appeared in the 1910s, but they were bulky and noisy, and their motors needed regular maintenance. In the 1920s a household machine could cost as much as a small car, and only the wealthiest families could consider buying one. Sealed motors, introduced at the end of that decade, made later models far more reliable, and mass production brought prices down steadily. By the 1950s most North American families owned a refrigerator, whereas in much of Europe it was still a sign of prosperity. Where homes lacked one, people shopped daily for fresh food, a habit that shaped the layout of towns, with small food shops on every corner.

F  Frozen food took longer still to win over shoppers. Early frozen vegetables, frozen slowly in large blocks, emerged from the packet as a watery mush, and customers rejected them. The solution was quick freezing. When food is frozen rapidly, the ice crystals that form are tiny and do little damage to the cell walls, so texture and flavour survive thawing. Once the method was adopted in the 1930s, frozen peas, fish and ready meals began to appear in the shops, and the home freezer, combined with the refrigerator, allowed families to buy in bulk and to eat out of season. Supermarkets, with their huge refrigerated displays, depended on these technologies, and in turn made them part of everyday life.

G  Today's food trade depends on an unbroken 'cold chain' of refrigerated warehouses, lorries, ships, shop displays and kitchens, each of which must hold its temperature. The chain has costs. The first chemicals used in cooling machines were found to damage the ozone layer, and their replacements are powerful greenhouse gases; refrigeration also consumes a significant share of the world's electricity. Meanwhile, the chain remains patchy where it is needed most. In some regions, as much as a third of perishable food spoils between farm and market for want of cold storage, a loss that better refrigeration could prevent. Engineers are now designing machines that run on solar power or on safer gases, hoping to extend the benefits of cold without its environmental price.

passages.title: Order Without a Leader
paras: A  An ant colony can contain a million individuals, and yet there is no manager among them. The queen lays eggs but issues no instructions; no ant has a plan of the nest, a map of the foraging area or a list of jobs to be filled. Even so, colonies build elaborate nests, find food efficiently, defend their territory and adjust to changing conditions. Each worker's brain holds only a few hundred thousand neurons, a tiny fraction of the number in a human brain, so the intelligence of a colony cannot be explained by the cleverness of its members. Biologists describe such behaviour as emergent: it arises from the interactions between many simple individuals, not from the decisions of any one of them.

B  The best-understood example is the way ants find food. A forager that discovers a source returns to the nest laying a trail of chemical signals called pheromones, and other ants, attracted by the scent, follow it and add their own. In a classic laboratory experiment, a nest was connected to a food source by a bridge with two branches, one twice as long as the other. At first ants used both branches equally, but within minutes most were using the shorter one. No ant had compared the two routes. Those on the shorter branch simply completed the round trip sooner, so their pheromone built up faster, attracting still more ants. The chemical also evaporates, so a trail that is no longer reinforced disappears, and the colony can abandon a source that has run out.

C  Deciding how many ants should forage, and how many should stay at home to clean the nest or tend the young, is a harder problem, and the research of Dr Imogen Falk on harvester ants suggests an elegant solution. At the nest entrance, foragers returning with food bump into those waiting to leave. An ant is more likely to set out when it meets returning foragers frequently, because frequent meetings mean that food is plentiful nearby. When few meet it, it stays inside. By touching antennae, the ants exchange chemical information about one another's jobs, and each responds to the rate of encounters rather than to any message from above. The result is that the colony sends out more foragers on good days and fewer on bad ones.

D  Colonies do not consist of identical workers. Individual ants differ in how readily they respond to a task: some are bold explorers, others cautious followers; some abandon a trail quickly, others persist. At first sight, such variation seems wasteful. Experiments suggest otherwise. When researchers removed foragers from a colony, workers that had previously patrolled took over their role, and colonies with a wide mix of temperaments recovered faster than those in which the workers were more alike. In a stable environment, uniformity might be efficient. In a changing one, variety gives the colony a reserve of different responses to draw on, and it is this reserve that allows it to adapt when conditions change.

E  Some species use their own bodies as building material. Army ants, which have no permanent home, link their legs to form bridges across gaps in the forest floor, and gather in clusters known as bivouacs in which the queen and larvae are sheltered. Fire ants, whose nests are often in flood plains, respond to rising water by clinging to one another, and the colony forms a raft that can float for weeks. No ant directs the construction. Each follows a simple rule: an ant that feels many others walking over it holds its position, while one that is not bearing weight moves on. Repeated across thousands of bodies, the rule produces a structure that bends, floats and repairs itself.

F  Self-organisation has its failures. Occasionally the leading ants in a column of army ants lose the scent and begin following the ants behind them, so that the trail closes into a circle. Because each ant follows the one in front, the column goes round and round, sometimes for days, until the exhausted insects die in their hundreds. Such ant mills were described by naturalists in the nineteenth century, and they remind us that the method is not infallible. A colony that commits early to a poor food source may also find it hard to change, since a strong trail is difficult to undo. The system favours speed and robustness over perfect accuracy, and most of the time this is a sensible compromise.

G  Computer scientists have borrowed these ideas. In ant colony optimisation, software agents wander through a network of possible solutions, leaving a digital pheromone on the better ones so that later agents are drawn towards them. The technique is now used by logistics companies to plan delivery routes and by telecommunications engineers to direct data through busy networks. Roboticists have built swarms of small, inexpensive machines that cooperate without central control; if one fails, the others carry on. Swarm robots remain largely experimental, however, and for most tasks a single large machine is still more efficient.

H  Enthusiasm for the ant colony as a model should be tempered by caution. Workers in a colony are close relatives, descended from a single queen, so their interests are closely aligned; humans, with their varied aims and rivalries, are in a very different position. Some management writers have urged companies to copy ants and abandon hierarchy, but most researchers consider this a misreading of the science. Ants, they point out, perform a narrow range of tasks in a fairly predictable world. What the insects offer is not a blueprint for human organisation but a reminder that complex order can arise without anyone being in charge.

passages.title: What Makes a Good Teacher?
paras: A  Ask adults to name the teacher who changed their lives and most can do so at once. Ask what, exactly, that teacher did, and the answers scatter: she was strict; he was funny; she never gave up on us; he made it all seem like a game. The ease of the first question and the difficulty of the second have frustrated education policymakers for decades. Convinced that the quality of teachers is the most important influence on pupils' progress that schools can control, governments have spent heavily on the search for what it consists of. They are right to be convinced: in the best classrooms, pupils learn months more each year than in the weakest. I shall argue, however, that the search has produced valuable evidence but also a seductive mistake, the belief that good teaching is a fixed set of traits that can be measured, rewarded and recruited for.

B  Begin with the most obvious candidates, qualifications and experience. Common sense says that teachers with more of both should do better, and pay scales in most countries assume it. The evidence is less tidy. Professor Lena Aldous followed the progress of some 40,000 pupils over six years and found that teachers improve noticeably during their first three years in the job, after which the gains flatten out. A degree in the subject taught made a difference in secondary mathematics but hardly anywhere else. Credentials, then, are a poor guide to who will excel, which is uncomfortable for systems that reward them with higher salaries and promotion, and which should make us wary of any policy built on the assumption that years of service and certificates tell us who is best.

C  Aldous's team also measured what are known as value-added scores: how much more or less progress a teacher's pupils make than similar pupils elsewhere. The differences were large; pupils of teachers in the top fifth gained roughly an extra three months of learning a year compared with those of teachers in the bottom fifth. Yet the scores proved unstable. A teacher ranked near the top one year could be found in the middle the next, because classes are small and results vary for reasons that have nothing to do with teaching. Averaged over several years, the scores tell us something real. Used to decide the career of an individual, they are, in my view, unacceptably unreliable.

D  Classroom observation seems a fairer alternative, and many systems rely on it. Dr Pieter Voss trained observers to rate lessons using a detailed checklist, then compared their ratings. He found that a teacher's score depended as much on who was watching, and on which lesson happened to be chosen, as on the teacher. Observation can be valuable, but only when observers are thoroughly trained and visit often, and that is costly. Few schools, in my experience, can afford to do it properly, and a single visit by a busy head teacher is little better than a guess, however confident the written report may sound. The danger is that an unreliable judgement, once recorded in a file, begins to be treated as fact.

E  The most underrated source of evidence is also the cheapest: the pupils themselves. A team led by Professor Ingrid Halvorsen asked 20,000 pupils to rate their teachers on statements such as 'My teacher explains difficult ideas clearly' and 'My teacher notices when I do not understand'. The ratings predicted how much the pupils went on to learn better than the scores given by adult observers. Sceptics fear that children simply reward teachers who are easy-going or entertaining, but the surveys suggested otherwise: pupils were quite able to tell the difference between a lesson that was fun and one that was useful, and they marked down teachers who were relaxed about discipline. Surveys of very young children are less dependable, but for older pupils I regard them as a resource that schools neglect.

F  What do the successful teachers in these studies share? Summaries of the research point to clear explanations, high expectations, regular feedback and a sound relationship with pupils. But even these findings should be handled with care. A style that works with one class may fail with another: a teacher who is firmly directive may suit anxious beginners yet frustrate confident, older pupils. The teachers I have most admired do not behave identically from one lesson to the next; they read the room and adjust. Good teaching is therefore better described as a series of judgements made in context than as a list of traits, and judgement, unlike a trait, can be developed.

G  That conclusion points towards a different kind of policy. Dr Marta Quispe ran a trial in which pairs of teachers observed one another's lessons and discussed what they saw, for one hour a fortnight. After two years, pupils in the participating schools had made modest but measurable gains, at very little cost. Financial incentives have fared worse: in trials in several countries, bonuses for results made little difference to pupils' progress. I remain unconvinced that they ever will. Money cannot buy skills that teachers have never been given the chance to learn. If we want better teaching, we should spend less on trying to identify the stars and more on helping every teacher to learn from colleagues, from pupils and from honest feedback.
